classification.difficultyReason: Turn the supplied triangle sum rule into subtraction recurrences, generalise a diagonal pattern algebraically, and extend it to the third and fourth diagonals using neighbouring-row formulas.

inlines.text: The configuration below is called the
. Notice that every entry is the sum of the two entries immediately below.

spec.sourceRegion: Left column, harmonic triangle beneath question 20
spec.description: Five widening rows of circular fraction entries. Each entry lies above the pair whose sum it equals. Decorative turquoise fills are omitted.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the five supplied rows are shown.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the entries in the next row.

answer.worked:
The first entry in row 6 is $\frac16$. Subtract successive entries from the entries above:
$$\begin{align*}\frac15-\frac16&=\frac1{30}\\\frac1{20}-\frac1{30}&=\frac1{60}\\\frac1{30}-\frac1{60}&=\frac1{60}\\\frac1{20}-\frac1{60}&=\frac1{30}\\\frac15-\frac1{30}&=\frac16.\end{align*}$$
The next row is $\frac16,\frac1{30},\frac1{60},\frac1{60},\frac1{30},\frac16$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: The entries in the first diagonal are the unit fractions: $\frac11,\frac12,\frac13,\frac14$, and so on. Find a pattern that gives the entries in the second diagonal.

answer.worked: The second-diagonal entries are $\frac12,\frac16,\frac1{12},\frac1{20},\ldots$. Their denominators are $2\times1,3\times2,4\times3,5\times4,\ldots$: multiply the row number by the preceding integer.

children.label: c
children.prompt: What fraction will appear in the second diagonal on the $n$th row? Can you prove it?

answer.short:
$\frac1{n(n-1)}$, for $n\ge2$.

Subtract the first entry in row $n$ from the first entry in row $n-1$.
answer.worked:
The first entry in row $n-1$ is the sum of the first two entries in row $n$. Thus the second entry in row $n$ is
$$\begin{align*}\frac1{n-1}-\frac1n&=\frac{n-(n-1)}{n(n-1)}\\\frac1{n-1}-\frac1n&=\frac1{n(n-1)}.\end{align*}$$
This proves the formula for every $n\ge2$. Equivalently, $\frac1n+\frac1{n(n-1)}=\frac1{n-1}$, the entry immediately above.

children.label: d
children.prompt: What about the entries in the third and fourth diagonal on the $n$th row?

answer.short:
Third: $\frac2{n(n-1)(n-2)}$ for $n\ge3$.

Fourth: $\frac6{n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)}$ for $n\ge4$. Subtract adjacent-diagonal entries using the sum rule.
answer.worked:
Each entry above is the sum of the two entries below. The third entry in row $n$ is therefore
$$\begin{align*}\frac1{(n-1)(n-2)}-\frac1{n(n-1)}&=\frac{n-(n-2)}{n(n-1)(n-2)}\\\frac1{(n-1)(n-2)}-\frac1{n(n-1)}&=\frac2{n(n-1)(n-2)}.\end{align*}$$
Similarly, the fourth entry is
$$\begin{align*}\frac2{(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)}-\frac2{n(n-1)(n-2)}&=\frac{2n-2(n-3)}{n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)}\\\frac2{(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)}-\frac2{n(n-1)(n-2)}&=\frac6{n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)}.\end{align*}$$
